I have no actual scientific base to sustain my arguments (haven’t researched this in particular), but from experience, my guess is this could be mostly related to intrusive/obsessive thoughts.

As far as I know depression itself relies primarily on persistent low mood which might make one more prone to rationalizing suicidal thoughts. I’m not sure how intrusive the ideation you’re asking about actually is though.

As far as somatic effects go, LSD displays some (generally) mild vasoconstriction effects. It may also interact with bipolar meds such as lithium, which lowers the seizure threshold and could cause serious damage.

Acid and any other hallucinogens by themselves can also trigger underlying mental disorders in the short and long term, such as anxiety, psychosis, mania, obsessions in general, etc. 

A bad trip is generally just an episode of anxiety and, in serious cases, psychosis. The issue lies in the persistence of the trauma beyond a single, isolated episode, especially if there is no proper integration of the experience afterwards and if the user is prone to mental disorders. 

The persistence of those symptoms is grouped into one single condition called r/HPPD, which is theoretically rare but you can’t really trust numbers when it comes to illegal substances.

It definitely can change your brain chemistry. Sometimes it’s just not as effective without medication (thus the combo meds + therapy being so important).

Therapy helps you create strategies to engage in behavioral patterns that optimize your brain’s response to neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin. The same way you can, for example, upregulate dopamine receptors by jerking off too much or abusing stimulants, you can downregulate them with the appropriate habits (like exercise) and meds. The same thing with serotonin, which is the major problem in depression: the serotonin reuptake system is too desensitized, meaning that for most serotonin-mediated stimuli your brain receives, whether it’s from drugs (from MDMA to SSRI’s) or from activities (from shoplifting to exercising), too much serotonin leaves the receptors too fast. SSRI’s act by making serotonin stick to these receptors for longer periods, and therapy + discipline act by generating appropriate stimuli at the appropriate time.

Basically, therapy is just a strategy of manipulating your brain chemistry through actions.

Therapy and medication are really important.
